The main components of a substation transformer include the core, windings, insulation, oil, and cooling system. The core is made up of thin laminations of steel, which are stacked together to form the magnetic circuit. The windings are the conductors that carry the electrical current, and are insulated from each other and the core to prevent short circuits. The insulation is typically made of paper or oil-impregnated pressboard, and is used to insulate the windings from each other and the core. The oil serves as both a coolant and insulator, and helps to prevent the transformer from overheating. The cooling system is used to remove the heat generated by the transformer during operation.

A de-energized DETC, or Dead Tank Circuit Breaker, is a safety device that is used to isolate the transformer from the power system during maintenance or fault conditions. It's like a parking brake for the transformer, but instead of stopping the rotation of the wheels, it stops the flow of electricity. The main components of a de-energized DETC include the contacts, the insulating system, the trip system, and the auxiliary system. The contacts are the metal components that make and break the electrical connection between the transformer and the power system. The insulating system is used to prevent electrical arcing between the contacts. The trip system is used to detect faults in the transformer and initiate the opening of the contacts. The auxiliary system is used to provide power to the trip system and other auxiliary circuits.
